scenes.tts: The adult cortex is divided into areas. The embryo's cortex shows no borders at all. So where do the areas come from?
scenes.visual: Title card: A Sheet with No Borders. An adult mouse brain seen from above, coloured areas, beside a smooth grey embryonic sheet. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: The adult cortex is divided into areas. The embryo's cortex shows no borders at all. So where do the areas come from?

scenes.tts: The cortex is the sheet of neurons on the surface of the forebrain.
scenes.visual: A mouse brain from the side; the outer sheet of the forebrain highlights.
scenes.narration: The cortex is the sheet of neurons on the surface of the forebrain.

scenes.tts: In nineteen oh nine, Korbinian Brodmann divided the human cortex into areas by how its cells were packed and layered.
scenes.caption: In 1909, Korbinian Brodmann divided the human cortex into areas by how its cells were packed and layered.
scenes.visual: A stained section with dense and sparse layers; numbered patches appear on a human brain outline. On screen: Brodmann, 1909.
scenes.narration: In 1909, Korbinian Brodmann divided the human cortex into areas by how its cells were packed and layered.

scenes.tts: Many of his borders match borders of function. His area seventeen is primary visual cortex, the first cortical stop for signals from the eyes.
scenes.caption: Many of his borders match borders of function. His area 17 is primary visual cortex, the first cortical stop for signals from the eyes.
scenes.visual: Area 17 lights up at the back of the human brain; an eye icon links to it.
scenes.narration: Many of his borders match borders of function. His area 17 is primary visual cortex, the first cortical stop for signals from the eyes.

scenes.tts: This lesson works in the mouse. Here is the map we will use throughout.
scenes.visual: Transition to one mouse hemisphere seen from above. This dorsal map is the recurring visual for every chapter.
scenes.narration: This lesson works in the mouse. Here is the map we will use throughout.

scenes.tts: Front to back runs from the nose end to the back of the head.
scenes.visual: A front-to-back arrow along the hemisphere, labelled front and back.
scenes.narration: Front to back runs from the nose end to the back of the head.

scenes.tts: The medial edge runs along the midline. The lateral edge is the outer side.
scenes.visual: A second arrow across the hemisphere, labelled medial at the midline and lateral at the outer edge.
scenes.narration: The medial edge runs along the midline. The lateral edge is the outer side.

scenes.tts: Motor cortex sits at the front.
scenes.visual: A coloured patch at the front, labelled motor.
scenes.narration: Motor cortex sits at the front.

scenes.tts: Somatosensory cortex, the touch area, sits in the middle. Inside it lies the barrel field, the whisker map.
scenes.visual: A middle patch labelled somatosensory; inside it, rows of small dots labelled barrel field, with a whiskered snout beside it.
scenes.narration: Somatosensory cortex, the touch area, sits in the middle. Inside it lies the barrel field, the whisker map.

scenes.tts: Auditory cortex sits on the lateral side, toward the back.
scenes.visual: A lateral patch toward the back, labelled auditory.
scenes.narration: Auditory cortex sits on the lateral side, toward the back.

scenes.tts: Visual cortex sits at the back.
scenes.visual: A patch at the back, labelled visual.
scenes.narration: Visual cortex sits at the back.

scenes.tts: We will call motor and somatosensory the front-and-middle areas. Visual is the back area.
scenes.visual: Motor and somatosensory patches bracket together as front-and-middle; the visual patch is labelled back area.
scenes.narration: We will call motor and somatosensory the front-and-middle areas. Visual is the back area.

scenes.tts: The cortex grows from a smooth sheet of progenitors, cells that divide to make neurons.
scenes.visual: Dividing cells across the sheet, all the same grey.
scenes.narration: The cortex grows from a smooth sheet of progenitors, cells that divide to make neurons.

scenes.tts: The sheet that will hold the whisker map and the visual map looks the same from front to back.
scenes.visual: Faint dashed outlines of the future areas flicker over the uniform sheet, then fade.
scenes.narration: The sheet that will hold the whisker map and the visual map looks the same from front to back.

scenes.tts: Making the areas from it is called arealization.
scenes.visual: On screen: arealization.
scenes.narration: Making the areas from it is called arealization.

scenes.tts: Signalling centres at the edges of the sheet are active by about embryonic day nine and a half. They keep signalling as the first neurons are made.
scenes.caption: Signalling centres at the edges of the sheet are active by about embryonic day 9.5. They keep signalling as the first neurons are made.
scenes.visual: Timeline segment lights: signalling centres, active by E9.5, the bar running on into the neurogenesis segment. Small glowing spots at the front and medial edges of the sheet.
scenes.narration: Signalling centres at the edges of the sheet are active by about embryonic day 9.5. They keep signalling as the first neurons are made.

scenes.tts: Progenitors make the cortex's neurons from about embryonic day eleven to seventeen.
scenes.caption: Progenitors make the cortex's neurons from about embryonic day 11 to 17.
scenes.visual: Timeline segment: neurogenesis, E11 to E17. Neurons pile up above the sheet.
scenes.narration: Progenitors make the cortex's neurons from about embryonic day 11 to 17.

scenes.tts: The thalamus is the relay station for signals from the eyes, ears and skin.
scenes.visual: A thalamus drawn below the hemisphere, with eye, ear and skin icons feeding it.
scenes.narration: The thalamus is the relay station for signals from the eyes, ears and skin.

scenes.tts: Which comes first: the neurons of the cortex, or the thalamic axons that reach them?
scenes.visual: Two markers wait above the timeline: neurons made, thalamic axons arrive. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: Which comes first: the neurons of the cortex, or the thalamic axons that reach them?

scenes.tts: The first neurons are born first. Thalamic axons reach the developing cortex around embryonic day fourteen to fifteen, and wait in the layer just under it. More neurons are still being made then. The axons grow into the cortex itself later, around birth.
scenes.caption: The first neurons are born first. Thalamic axons reach the developing cortex around embryonic day 14 to 15, and wait in the layer just under it. More neurons are still being made then. The axons grow into the cortex itself later, around birth.
scenes.visual: Timeline segment: thalamic axons reach the cortex around E14 to E15 and wait in the subplate, overlapping the neurogenesis bar. Axon bundles grow up from the thalamus and pause just beneath the sheet, then enter it near birth.
scenes.narration: The first neurons are born first. Thalamic axons reach the developing cortex around embryonic day 14 to 15, and wait in the layer just under it. More neurons are still being made then. The axons grow into the cortex itself later, around birth.

scenes.tts: Barrels can be seen in the first postnatal week, around postnatal day four.
scenes.caption: Barrels can be seen in the first postnatal week, around postnatal day 4.
scenes.visual: Timeline segment: barrels visible, around P4. Dots in the barrel field sharpen into rows.
scenes.narration: Barrels can be seen in the first postnatal week, around postnatal day 4.

scenes.tts: So the sheet is already patterned and making neurons before the thalamic axons arrive.
scenes.visual: The whole timeline glows, with a bracket over the stretch before axons arrive.
scenes.narration: So the sheet is already patterned and making neurons before the thalamic axons arrive.

scenes.tts: Where do the borders come from, in a sheet that shows none?
scenes.visual: Card one: where do the borders come from?
scenes.narration: Where do the borders come from, in a sheet that shows none?

scenes.tts: What tells a progenitor where it sits, and can that be changed so a border moves?
scenes.visual: Card two: what tells a progenitor where it sits?
scenes.narration: What tells a progenitor where it sits, and can that be changed so a border moves?

scenes.tts: And what does input from the thalamus add, if the sheet has already been marked?
scenes.visual: Card three: what does thalamic input add?
scenes.narration: And what does input from the thalamus add, if the sheet has already been marked?

scenes.tts: The takeaway: the areas are real, and the embryonic sheet shows no borders for them. The next chapters ask what draws them, and when.
scenes.visual: The smooth sheet beside the adult map, a question mark between them. On screen: no borders yet.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: the areas are real, and the embryonic sheet shows no borders for them. The next chapters ask what draws them, and when.
